papers.title: MINT infers the latent single-cell spatial transcriptome from paired histology
papers.summary: MINT is a computational method that infers single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomic data by combining paired histology images with existing spatial transcriptomics data. It leverages the structural and morphological information in histology slides to predict gene expression at single-cell precision, even in regions where transcriptomic measurements are sparse or lower resolution. This approach aims to bridge the gap between imaging data and molecular profiling, enabling richer spatial maps of gene expression across tissue sections.
papers.why: This tool could enhance spatial transcriptomic resolution in brain tissue, potentially enabling more precise mapping of interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net-associated gene expression at single-cell resolution when paired with histology images.

papers.title: CUBE: Multimodal Representation Learning Reveals Biological Structure Across Histomorphology, Spatial Protein Phenotypes, and Transcriptome-Associated Signals
papers.summary: CUBE is a computational method that uses multimodal representation learning to integrate histology images, spatial protein data, and transcriptome-associated signals into a unified analysis framework. It aims to reveal shared biological structure across these different data types collected from the same tissue samples. The approach likely uses deep learning to align and jointly embed these modalities, helping researchers discover patterns that wouldn't be visible from any single data type alone.
papers.why: This multimodal AI framework could offer a template for integrating spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, and imaging data to jointly analyze mitophagy markers, interneuron subtypes, and perineuronal net structures in brain tissue.

papers.title: Selective depletion of upper-layer somatostatin interneuron subtypes in schizophrenia
papers.summary: This study investigates somatostatin-expressing interneurons in the brain and finds that specific subtypes located in the upper cortical layers are selectively lost or reduced in schizophrenia. The researchers likely used molecular and anatomical profiling to distinguish interneuron subtypes and quantify their depletion across cortical layers. The findings suggest that schizophrenia pathology involves cell-type- and layer-specific vulnerability among inhibitory interneurons rather than uniform loss.
papers.why: This work on subtype- and layer-specific vulnerability of somatostatin interneurons is highly relevant to understanding interneuron pathology and could inform spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic approaches to studying mitophagy/autophagy dysfunction and perineuronal net changes in disease-affected cortical circuits.

papers.title: Spatial isoform sequencing at single-cell resolution reveals cell-type-specific spatial isoform variability in multiple brain cell types.
papers.summary: This paper introduces a spatial isoform sequencing method that works at single-cell resolution in brain tissue. It shows that different cell types in the brain express distinct RNA isoforms depending on their spatial location. The technique combines spatial transcriptomics with long-read sequencing to capture isoform-level diversity across brain cell types, including neurons.
papers.why: Understanding cell-type-specific spatial isoform variability could reveal how interneurons and other neuronal populations regulate autophagy/mitophagy-related transcripts differently depending on their microenvironment, such as perineuronal net-associated niches.

papers.title: spaCraft: calibrated power analysis and sample-size planning for multi-sample spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: spaCraft is a proposed statistical tool for calibrating power analysis and planning sample sizes when designing spatial transcriptomics experiments that involve multiple samples. It aims to help researchers determine how many samples or replicates are needed to reliably detect spatial gene expression differences. This addresses a common experimental design gap in spatial omics studies where underpowered or overpowered designs waste resources or miss real effects.
papers.why: Rigorous sample-size planning with spatial transcriptomics power analysis would help design well-powered experiments studying interneuron and perineuronal net changes across brain regions.

papers.title: Striatal interneuron microcircuits gate reinforcement to stabilize adaptive choice
papers.summary: This paper investigates how microcircuits formed by striatal interneurons regulate reinforcement learning signals to support stable, adaptive decision-making. It likely examines how specific interneuron populations modulate dopamine-related reward signals or medium spiny neuron activity during choice tasks. The study probably combines circuit-level physiology or optogenetics with behavioral choice paradigms to show how interneuron gating prevents maladaptive shifts in learned behavior.
papers.why: Although focused on striatal circuits rather than the brain regions typically studied in this project, the paper's emphasis on interneuron microcircuit function could offer conceptual or methodological insights relevant to understanding interneuron roles and perineuronal net-associated circuit stability elsewhere in the brain.

papers.title: Median raphe input to dorsal CA1 shapes VIP interneuron recruitment and novelty-guided spatial memory
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the median raphe nucleus sends inputs to the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus, and how these inputs influence the activity of VIP-expressing interneurons. The study links this circuit to how the brain processes novel spatial information and forms spatial memories. It highlights a specific neuromodulatory pathway that shapes interneuron recruitment during exploration of new environments.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it examines VIP interneuron circuit dynamics in the hippocampus, which connects to the profile's focus on interneurons and their role in modulating neuronal networks, even though it does not directly address mitophagy, autophagy, perineuronal nets, or spatial omics.
